_: The half of a release manifest that no tool can measure: how far each board and each capability has actually been taken, and what a release of this firmware does not do. tools/release_manifest.py merges it with what it can read off a build. Everything here is a claim somebody has to keep true, so it is short, and every entry names where the evidence is.

pico2_w.note: The board these transcripts were taken on: provisioned, joined, granted, configured, revoked and reset.

pico_w.note: The same firmware for the RP2040. It builds for this board and has never been run on one, and the figure to look at before anybody does is what it leaves: 168,832 bytes of static RAM on a part with 270,336, against 168,448 on one with 532,480.

pico2.note: Run as pico-cablato over scripts/pico_bridge.py: online, configured twice, events journalled, a killed bridge seen as offline, a watchdog reset recovered.

pico.note: The wired build for the RP2040. It builds for this board and has never been run on one.

sensors.note: gpio, adc, onewire and the board's own temperature. A pin has been read, debounced and reported, but by the board driving its own pad: no PIR, no contact and no DS18B20 has ever answered.

presence.note: One iBeacon, watched for a thousand sightings in one room. An address-based watch is written and tested but has never followed a phone, which rotates its address.

audio.note: The I2S receiver has run for minutes with the blocks unbroken and the silence measuring as silence, on three pins that have never had a microphone on them. The live stream to the hub is proved against the hub's own gateway, not against a room.

bridge.note: A board with no radio, carried over USB by scripts/pico_bridge.py. The bridge publishes under the node's own certificate and decides nothing.

snapshot.note: PICO-10. It needs an SPI camera with a JPEG FIFO, and no such module has been on this board; nothing in this firmware pretends there is one. video.start is refused by name.

limitations: Every board here is experimental in the hub's own catalogue, and shown that way. No board has been through an acceptance matrix.
A power cut, as opposed to a reset. Everything proved so far used the watchdog, which resets the chip without taking the power off it.
Keeping the time, as opposed to getting it once. A board up for a day and the drift between two answers are unexamined.

A certificate listed as revoked is not refused: there is no CRL in this configuration, and revocation is the registry and the access list. Four other bad certificates have been offered to the broker and refused; none of them from the board itself.
Four of the six reset reasons are read from bits nothing here has set, and an RP2040 cannot tell a brown-out from a power-on at all.
Every event goes out with queued_ms 0: the queue does not record when a reading was put in it.
